content.title: Responses to Weaknesses
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their review. We provide answers to their questions below that we hope help clarify our work.

1.The authors mention that “we focus on quantum vision transformers applied to image classification tasks”. Can the authors explain more about why previous quantum transformers are not suitable for image classification task? What makes this work perform well in the classification task rather than others?

Originally, transformers have been applied to NLP tasks using an encoder-decoder architecture that embeds the words using the encoder, mixes the embeddings using transformers and decodes everything to perform some task. Later on, this approach has been adapted to computer vision by replacing words with patches extracted from some image. The attention mechanism remains mainly the same but the overall architecture is quite changed. The classical vision transformer inserts the attention mechanism in an architecture design specifically for vision. Whilst in NLP, words are processed sequentially, in vision we process and apply attention on all embeddings together. In other words, while all transformers use some attention mechanism, the overall architecture changes depending on the task. The main difference between our work and the few previous works is that previous work would exchange the classical neural networks with variational circuits and keep the same classical attention mechanism which then used in an NLP architecture. Here, we defined new quantum layers, a quantum attention mechanism, and we put everything within a vision transformer architecture. We also defined a novel and solely quantum way to perform vision tasks through the compound transformer.

2.Some figure captions are not clear. For example, what does \theta refer to in Fig. 4-6? Also, what does different lines stand for? What does the panel in Fig. 7-9 mean?

We will make the captions clearer. \theta is the parameter of the RBS gate as defined in Equation 1. Fig 7-9 provide the quantum circuits that consist of RBS gates for the different orthogonal layers.

3.What’s the motivation of introducing second-order compound matrix?

The second order compound matrix is the mathematical way to describe rigorously what happens when we use a pyramid/butterfly layer on an input that is a superposition of states with Hamming weight 2. In the compound Transformer, we took the idea of the classical Transformer that one needs to mix all different patches of the image and give different attention to each one of them, and defined a quantum way to perform something in the same spirit: here we load optimally all patches in uniform superposition and then perform a unitary that changes the attention we give to each one of them. To mathematically describe exactly what operation is performed in our layer, we need the second-order compound matrix formalism.

4.What are the differences between A- Orthogonal Patch-wise scheme (Table 2) and the classical transformer? It seems that both can be formulated as Vx_i.

The classical transformer also has the attention mechanism on top of performing VX. The orthogonal patch-wise does not include any attention mechanism. One can define a classical patch-wise model without attention as well using VX, then the difference would be just the orthogonality property.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors endeavor to design and test a quantum transformer (QT) architecture for image classification tasks. They propose three types of QT of increasing complexity. Classical data is loaded using a quantum matrix loader, a generalization of a quantum vector data loader. The features then extracted using quantum orthogonal layers. Three types of orthogonal layers are tested (butterfly, pyramid, and X, corresponding to different hardware conenctivity). Then  quantum attention layers are applied that vary from a close analogue of a classical attention layer to more quantumly versions. The architectures are tested on medical MNIST data and the authors conclude that the quantum counterparts of transformers require fewer parameters to achieve performance comparable to classical.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
The paper tackles in an innovative manner a very exciting problem of porting the latest, highly performant AI models (transformers) to the quantum domain. It offers a plethora of design choices (3 for for the fully connected orthogonal and 3 for the attention layers), extensive experiments with complex data and comparisons with prior art.. 


Weaknesses
The paper sort of sweeps under the carpet the fact that their architectures in fact are hybrid quantum-classical as they require classical nonlinearities, and the training is performed 
Also the authors do not discuss the limitations of the quantum instantiation of transformers as compared to the classical counterparts.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is written quite lucidly and provides needed background knowledge in the appendices.
It strikes as a highly innovative and original work that has a high impact potential.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this is a very exciting and compelling study aiming at proting classical transformer architectures to the quantum domain.

content.title: Reply to Weaknesses and other reviewer comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their review. We would like to provide some answers/remarks below. 

Weakness 1: As is stated in Fig. 6 in the paper, the encoding of a matrix X of size nd (n rows, d columns) requires a quantum circuit of O(n+d) qubits, O(nlogd+logn) depth and O(nd) gates which does not scale exponentially but only linearly with the size of the matrix nd. In fact, the number of gates is asymptotically optimal for any circuit that can encode any matrix of size nd. We will make this clearer in the paper so there is no misunderstanding. We agree with the reviewer that an exponential scaling would have made the results much weaker, but in our work, it is not the case.

Weakness 2: We will include more references on image classification in general. We restricted our references more on the ones that deal specifically with transformer architectures and not all possible papers about image classification. We will add the suggested references and more. 

Novelty: This is the first time that compound layers and also orthogonal transformer architectures have been defined and rigorously tested on a suite of 12 different medical image datasets. We believe that this is both technically and empirically novel.

Clarity: We will make all efforts to make the main text clearer and respect the page limit at the same time. Evidently, many technical things must remain in the Appendix due to space constraints.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a quantum version of vision transformer based on quantum approximation and quantum flavored (compound transformer). The paper evaluated using quantum simulation and actual IBM quantum hardware. The major contribution of the paper is a demonstration of attention layer implementation using orthogonal neural network and compound matrix. Note that those concepts are proposed on the prior works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The major strength are 1) two major direction of quantum attention computation, 2) demonstrated on various Med MNIST dataset. 

The major weakness is that although it is comparable or slightly better results than the classical counterpart, the demonstration of quantum advantage is questionable. As ViT paper explained that only after 100M training images, they could beat CNN based algorithm. There are emphirical and theoretical evidence of quantum advantages but on this paper, Quantum version of ViT (QViT) is not beating classical ResNET-18. 
Note that this is expected results and I admire the authors to try with small amount of data to show QViT demonstration. 

I understand that 32 qubit simulation is not cheap and actual quantum computer evaluation on one of MedMNIST data would be quite time consuming and expensive. Actually, the resulted presented in this paper is matched to my expected outcomes of the best outcomes from the small benchmark dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper was not written clearly. For instance, $n$ and $d$ are defined later in the paper and when I review the paper, I was quite confused and realized that they used $n$ and $d$ are all 16, which is fine but the authors should define before they used the variables. 

Another is that there are four quantum approximation methods proposed but they tested three and I understand now 
but the statements are not consistent. 

The overall presentation of the paper could be significantly improved and when the authors submitted ICLR, I felt the authors rushed reformat archive version and didn't go through the details, which may cause clarity concerns. 

In terms of reproducibility, I have a bigger concern that the authors refuse to share the code. Authors claimed that it's fairly easy but then why not sharing fairly easy one to let others to reproduce the work. I check the authors the cited work on previous ICLR submission, and it got the same review's point.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper has a value to QML community. However, as I pointed out in weakness, this would be tough topic to be validated and thus I'm more leaning toward reject than accept, which takes into account of the reproducibility of the proposed work.

content.title: Reply to reviewer's comments/questions
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their review. We would like to provide some answers/remarks below. 

Weakness: We want to first remark that for us the main goal and contribution of the paper is defining quantum transformers that theoretically make sense, scale well and also provide good experimental results. In particular, for the experimental results we were actually very positively surprised that even for these small scale simulations of the quantum architectures that we could perform on classical computers we managed to show i) that our quantum transformers can consistently outperform classical transformers for these datasets (which also gives as hope that they will continue to outperform classical Transformers for the much larger datasets where Transformers start beating CNNs) and ii) for the smaller datasets and in particular for the RetinaMNIST (which we focused on for the hardware experiments and performed a more extensive hyperparameter optimization) we indeed also beat ResNet-18 both on simulation and on the hardware! (as we did also for PneumoniaMNIST), even though the quantum transformer has a few hundreds of parameters versus the 11 millions of ResNet. We also decided to be very clear about all the results and not only pick the datasets where we outperformed these classical architectures and indeed for most other datasets, the quantum transformers need to be larger to compete with ResNets. As the reviewer says, the effort to perform such extensive simulations and experiments is great and we strongly believe that the results are convincing that in the future such quantum transformers with larger size will be a great addition to classical methods and provide models that at times can provide better models.

Clarity: We will make all efforts to clarify things in the final version of the paper respecting the space constraints, including defining the dimensions and clarifying the number of methods (there are three different models, the quantum attention circuit is just a quantum way of doing the inference given the attention coefficients. We have performed experiments on the quantum hardware which uses quantum attention as well.)

Reproducibility: We are going to make available the trained models including the quantum circuits (in qiskit format) so that the hardware experiments and inference simulations can be readily reproduced.
